question: to the Commission Thijs Reuten (S&D), Chloé Ridel (S&D), Barry Andrews (Renew), Tineke Strik (Verts/ALE), Catarina Vieira (Verts/ALE) Subject:

We note the ‘Declaration by the EU and its Member States in support of effective multilateralism’ (2 September 2026). While welcoming the commitments outlined in the declaration, we see a persistent gap in the actions of the Commission regarding the International Criminal Court (ICC). Specifically, the Declaration ‘underlines […] the need to preserve and protect [the ICC’s] independence, impartiality and effective functioning free from pressure, intimidation or interference’, therefore implicitly recognising threats to these principles. The United States administration has sanctioned the ICC, several of its judges, the Chief Prosecutor, and ICC staff, as well as non-governmental organisations that support the ICC’s work, and has launched a whole-of-government campaign to dismantle it. The Declaration gives the EU a mandate to act. The Parliament has repeatedly called for the Blocking Statute1 to be activated. However, the Commission has neither taken appropriate action to help protect the ICC, nor responded adequately to the Parliament’s questions and resolutions on this matter. 1.
Does the Commission consider that the United States’ sanctions and threats affect the ICC’s independence, impartiality and effective functioning?
If so, what action has the Commission taken in response, and if it has not acted, why not?
If not, what would need to occur to meet the threshold for the ICC to be considered affected?

Council Regulation (EC) No 2271/96 of 22 November 1996 protecting against the effects of the extraterritorial application of legislation adopted by a third country, and actions based thereon or resulting therefrom (OJ L 309, 29.11.1996, p. 1, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/1996/2271/oj). 1
